title: Under the Neem Tree

sections.heading: Beginning
sections.content:
The Zilla Parishad school stood at the edge of the village like a bright blue-and-white box, its walls freshly painted before every monsoon. A large neem tree grew in the courtyard, spreading its branches wide like open arms. Every morning, children gathered under it for assembly, and at lunchtime, they sat in neat rows with steel plates for the midday meal.

Sanika Jadhav loved this school. She loved the dusty playground, the smell of chalk, and most of all, she loved drawing. Her pencil box was stuffed with colored pencils — twelve of them — and she could draw anything: birds, flowers, the Sahyadri hills that rose behind the village like sleeping giants.

One Tuesday morning, their teacher Kavita Bai walked into class with a big smile. She clapped her hands twice, and everyone fell silent.

"Listen carefully, children," she said. "Our school has been chosen to participate in the taluka-level 'Best Village Display' competition. It will happen during Bail Pola week!"

The class buzzed with excitement. Bail Pola was everyone's favorite festival — the day when families decorated their bullocks with colorful beads and painted horns, fed them sweet puran poli, and paraded them through the village with dhol-tasha drums.

"Each class must prepare a project showing something special about our village," Bai continued. "I want you to work in groups."

Sanika's hand shot up immediately. "Bai, can we draw charts? I can make beautiful pictures!"

"Of course, Sanika. But remember, a good project needs more than pretty pictures. It needs truth."

In the back row, Rohit Kale sat quietly, looking at his hands. He was a thin boy with sun-darkened skin and careful eyes that noticed everything — the direction of the wind, the color of the clouds, the mood of a bullock. But in the classroom, he felt invisible.

During the lunch break, Sanika opened her small steel tiffin box. Inside were two round bhakri made from jowar flour, a small container of spicy green thecha, and some yogurt. She ate happily under the neem tree.

Nearby, Aniket Shinde was talking loudly to his friends. "What will Rohit do for the project?" he said, laughing. "He only knows about mud and bullocks. This is a school competition, not a farming competition!"

Some boys laughed. Rohit heard them. He pressed his lips together, packed his half-eaten lunch back into his tiffin, and walked away toward the school wall, where he sat alone.

sections.heading: Middle
sections.content:
Bai divided the class into four groups. Sanika's group had six children, and they decided to make their project about the village's farming life.

"I'll draw the sugarcane fields!" Sanika announced. "And someone can draw the river, and someone can write about the crops."

For three days, the group worked hard. Sanika painted bright green fields and golden jowar stalks on chart paper. Another girl, Priya, wrote neat paragraphs about the village. But when they pinned everything on the display board, something felt wrong.

"It looks nice," Priya said slowly, "but it looks like a picture from a textbook. It doesn't feel like our village."

Sanika stared at the board and knew Priya was right. The drawings were colorful, but they were empty — like a beautiful box with nothing inside.

That same afternoon, after school, the children played lagori on the open ground near the Maruti temple. Teams from neighboring houses gathered, stacking seven flat stones and trying to knock them down with a ball. Aniket led one team, shouting instructions like a little captain.

Rohit didn't play. He walked home along the red soil path, past the soybean fields, to help his father load sugarcane onto the bullock cart. His two bullocks, Shiva and Ganya, greeted him with soft snorts. He rubbed their foreheads gently.

"Baba, when do we start preparing Shiva and Ganya for Pola?" Rohit asked his father.

"Soon, soon. Your ajoba is already carving new wooden toys for the little ones in the village."

Rohit smiled. His grandfather sat on the veranda every evening, carving tiny bullock figures from neem wood with his old knife. Each one was perfect — the curved horns, the strong legs, the little wooden yoke.

The next morning, Rohit came to school carrying a cloth bag. Inside were a small piece of sugarcane stalk, a handful of dried jowar grains, and two tiny hand-carved wooden bullocks his grandfather had made. He placed them quietly on his desk.

Sanika noticed. She walked over and picked up one of the wooden bullocks. "Rohit, this is beautiful! Your grandfather made this?"

Rohit nodded shyly.

"What's in the bag?" she asked.

He showed her the sugarcane and the jowar grains. "I thought... maybe someone could use them. For the project."

Sanika's eyes went wide. "Rohit, this is exactly what we need! Our project has drawings but no real things. Will you join our group?"

Rohit looked down. "Aniket said farmers' sons don't know about competitions."

Sanika shook her head firmly. "Aniket is wrong. Your knowledge is the most important part of our project. You know things none of us know."

Rohit hesitated for a long moment. Then he nodded.

From that day, the project transformed. Rohit explained the cycle of farming — how his father plowed the field before the monsoon, sowed soybean seeds in June, and harvested jowar in the winter. He described how the soil smelled different before rain, like wet iron and fresh leaves. Sanika listened carefully and painted each season in bright colors on the chart paper.

Rohit placed the real sugarcane stalk and jowar grains on the display board next to Sanika's paintings. He set his grandfather's wooden bullocks in the center, with a small card that read: "Our bullocks help us farm. On Bail Pola, we thank them."

Other children wanted to help too. Priya brought her mother's thecha recipe written on a card — green chilies, garlic, peanuts, and salt, ground on a stone. A boy named Vishal brought a photograph of decorated bullocks from last year's Pola celebration, their horns painted orange and green, necklaces of marigolds around their thick necks.

Even Aniket walked over one day. He stood looking at the display for a long time.

"That's Shiva and Ganya, isn't it?" he asked Rohit, pointing at the wooden bullocks.

Rohit nodded.

"They look exactly right," Aniket said quietly. "My father's dairy cows are not this handsome." He paused. "Can I add something? My mother makes the best ukdiche modak in the village. I can bring the recipe."

"Yes!" Sanika said. "Everyone should add something."

Bai watched all of this from her desk, smiling.

sections.heading: End
sections.content:
The day of the taluka competition arrived on a bright, clear morning. Judges from the Block Education Office came in a white car and walked through the school, visiting each classroom's display.

When they reached Sanika and Rohit's class, they stopped. The display board was alive with color and truth. Sanika's paintings showed the four seasons of farming — plowing, sowing, growing, and harvesting. Real jowar grains were glued in neat rows. A piece of sugarcane stood in a small clay pot. The wooden bullocks sat proudly in the center, and around them were recipe cards, photographs, and a hand-drawn map of the village showing every field and path.

"Who will explain this?" asked one of the judges, a tall woman with kind eyes.

Rohit stepped forward. His heart was beating fast, but when he looked at the display — at his grandfather's bullocks, at the jowar his family had grown — he felt a warmth rise in his chest. This was his world. He knew it well.

"This is our village," he began, his voice steady. "We grow sugarcane, soybean, and jowar. My father wakes up before sunrise and takes the bullock cart to the field. The soil here is red, and before the monsoon comes, it smells like iron."

He picked up the wooden bullock. "My ajoba carved this. On Bail Pola, we decorate our bullocks because they work hard all year. We paint their horns, put bead necklaces on them, and feed them puran poli — sweet flatbread stuffed with jaggery and lentils. Then we parade them through the village with dhol-tasha music. It is our way of saying thank you."

Sanika stood beside him, pointing to her illustrations as he spoke. When Rohit finished, the judges clapped.

That afternoon, the results were announced. Rohit and Sanika's class won second prize — a set of twenty books for the school library. The children cheered so loudly that birds flew out of the neem tree.

But something even better happened. After the competition, Aniket walked up to Rohit and said, "You knew more than all of us. I'm sorry I said those things."

Rohit smiled. "It's okay. You helped too, with the modak recipe."

Three days later, Bail Pola arrived. Rohit's family woke before dawn. His mother made puran poli while his father and grandfather decorated Shiva and Ganya. They painted the bullocks' horns bright red and yellow, hung necklaces of colorful beads around their necks, and draped embroidered cloth over their backs.

Sanika came running down the red soil path to Rohit's house, her skirt swishing, her eyes shining. "They look magnificent!" she cried.

The whole village gathered as families paraded their bullocks through the streets. The dhol-tasha players beat their drums, and the sound echoed off the Sahyadri hills. Children danced and clapped. Rohit walked proudly beside Shiva and Ganya, and Sanika walked with him.

Afterward, they sat under the neem tree at Rohit's house, eating warm puran poli with their hands, laughing and talking about the competition.

At school the next day, Bai stood before the class. She looked at each child slowly and said, "You have all learned something important. Sanika's drawings were beautiful, but without Rohit's knowledge, they were just pictures. Rohit's knowledge was deep, but without Sanika's art, it had no voice. And without all of you adding your pieces, the project would not have won."

She paused and smiled.

"No knowledge is small. The child who knows the earth knows the world."

Rohit sat at his desk, and for the first time all year, he did not feel invisible. He felt seen.

characters.name: Sanika Jadhav
characters.role: A creative, kind 9-year-old girl who loves drawing and brings the project to life with her art. She recognizes Rohit's value and invites him to join her group.

characters.name: Rohit Kale
characters.role: A quiet, observant 10-year-old boy who helps his family farm sugarcane and soybean. His deep knowledge of farming and nature becomes the heart of the school project.

characters.name: Kavita Bai
characters.role: The warm and wise teacher at the Zilla Parishad school who encourages every child to contribute and believes all knowledge has value.

characters.name: Aniket Shinde
characters.role: A mischievous, competitive classmate who initially teases Rohit but later apologizes and contributes to the project, showing that people can change.

vocabulary_words.context_sentence: Rohit hesitated for a long moment. Then he nodded.
vocabulary_words.simple_definition: Paused before doing something because of feeling unsure or nervous.

vocabulary_words.context_sentence: From that day, the project transformed.
vocabulary_words.simple_definition: Changed completely into something much better or different.
Extremely beautiful and impressive to look at.

vocabulary_words.context_sentence: But in the classroom, he felt invisible.
vocabulary_words.simple_definition: Feeling like nobody can see you or notice you are there.

vocabulary_words.context_sentence: The whole village gathered as families paraded their bullocks through the streets.
vocabulary_words.simple_definition: Walked together in a group through a public place to celebrate or show something.

moral_lesson: Working together and respecting every person's contribution — no matter how small — helps the whole community succeed. True friendship means lifting others up rather than competing against them. No knowledge is small; every person's life experience is valuable.
